items.html: The most common Hawaii licence plate is white with an arcing rainbow across the centre of the plate. When blurred, you can sometimes see the outline of the rainbow. Front plates are required in Hawaii.

Hawaii is the only state to use its own language, though English is still predominantly used. Most place names are in Hawaiian, so you can spot it on street signs, and other road markers.

  • Hawaiian is a vowel-oriented language that only uses eight consonants: H, K, L, M, N, P, W, and (ʻ), called an ʻOkina.
  • Every Hawaiian word ends in one of 5 vowels: A, E, I, O, or U.
  • Each vowel can also have a macron) over it: Ā, Ē, Ī, Ō, and Ū.

These vowels are often combined to make Diphthongs. I.e. UI, AI, AE, etc...

Hawaii has a large amount of Generation 4 "smallcam" coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front, with parts of the car being visible. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

Hawaii is known for its lush and tropical vegetation, with a variety of plants and trees. However, being a volcanic island chain, Hawaii has a wide range of landscapes, and as such vegetation as well.

You will often see plenty of ferns, tall grass, or other flowers on the sides of the roads.

Topography on Hawaii is characterised by many sloping volcanoes, rugged cliffs, hills, valleys and craters. Such distinct topography combined with tropical vegetation is a good way to identify Hawaii.
Contemporary Hawaiian homes are typically 1 or 2 storey wooden structures, commonly lighter in colour. Many homes feature retaining walls made of volcanic rock.

Thick yellow bands can sometimes be seen on poles in Hawaii.

NOTE: Make sure not to confuse this with the 3 stripes found on Californian poles.
Hawaii uses highway shields that resemble a guitar pick, with the numbers on the bottom of the shield. Most highway signs also use yellow signposts.

A stubby antenna can be seen in most Generation 3 coverage on Hawaii.

NOTE: The antenna is not always visible, so make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

Hawaii has a fair amount of Generation 2 coverage, compared to other US states. Especially on more rural roads.

NOTE: Generation 2 can be recognized by the lower quality camera, and circular blur above and below the camera.
Raised pavement markers in Hawaii will commonly be placed in a specific pattern: a single reflector, followed by four reflectors put close together and then a single reflector, repeating the pattern.

State highways are grouped by their first digit, with 1 and 2 found on Hawaiʻi, 3 on Maui, 4 on Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi, 5 on Kauaʻi and 6 to 9 on Oʻahu.

Moreover, all four of the so-called interstate highways are located on Oʻahu.
On the three largest islands, namely Hawaiʻi, Maui and Oʻahu, smallcam coverage was taken with a black Google car.
Smallcam imagery on the islands of Kauaʻi, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi was captured by a white car. Just like with the black car, you will often be able to see the unblurred hood and mirrors.
Generation 2 and non-smallcam Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the islands of Hawaiʻi, Maui and Oʻahu. The other islands only have Generation 3 or smallcam coverage.

The Island of Kauaʻi is the furthest west island in Hawaii with official Google coverage. This island has deep red soil and has large rugged hills with lush, jungle-like vegetation.

NOTE: Other islands such as Maui and Molokaʻi have similar soil colours, but the hillsides on them will typically have less dense vegetation.

The Island of Oʻahu lies southeast of Kauaʻi. It is known for being home to the Honolulu urban area. It also is home to steep, lush hills, which can be commonly seen from all around the island, especially in Honolulu’s suburbs.
Honolulu, located on southern Oʻahu, is by far the largest city and urban area in Hawaii. If you are in a dense urban area and can see tall buildings, you will always be in or near Honolulu.

The Island of Molokaʻi is just southeast of Oʻahu. It features deep red soil and a prominent volcano on the eastern end of the island. Especially in the older Generation 3 coverage, the vegetation appears very dry. Molokaʻi is also very sparsely populated.

The Island of Lānaʻi is a small, yet distinct island that lies just south of Moloka’i. A volcano is found just east of the centre of the island, adjacent to the town of Lānaʻi. In this area, tall Cook pines are abundant. In addition, some main roads near the centre of the island are lined with younger Cook pines.
Towards the coasts of the island of Lānaʻi, hills dotted with dry grass and shrubby vegetation are commonly seen. These areas are very rural with few buildings.
The Island of Maui sits southeast of Molokaʻi. In the centre of the island, you will find dry and somewhat flat grasslands with one or both of the mountain ranges on the island visible.
Coastal areas of Maui are noticeably more lush and green. Banana plants, palm trees, and views of the mountains are all common.

The Island of Hawai’i (also referred to as The Big Island) is both the largest and farthest southeast island with Street View coverage in the state. The interior areas feature rolling, grassy plains and volcanic rocks. You can typically see one or more of the island’s volcanoes from the road.

The coastal areas of the island of Hawai’i are where most of the towns and built-up areas on the island are located. These areas are typically more lush and have more trees and fern plants than the interior.

Rural roads going through forests within a flat landscape are commonly found south of the city of Hilo, on the island of Hawaiʻi.

NOTE: Mountainous forests are dotted around Hawaii, but if you are in one, and you see red soil with Generation 3, consider guessing in Kauaʻi, the westernmost covered island.
Within Hawaii, a distinct green blur can only be seen on the island of Oʻahu.

The infamous “Hawaiian lattice” can be recognized by the volcanic soil and rocks that are abundant in the region. Volcanic vegetation can also be seen lining the roads. Note that the angle of the roads is a big clue for the area, and that this lattice was built on the slope of Mauna Loa.
The town of Kaunakakai is the largest settlement on the Island of Molokaʻi. It is the only area on the island with an ‘urban’ vibe. As it is on Molokaʻi, the soil is somewhat red.
The Red Hill can easily be recognised by this unique barren, red rocky landscape. Due to the high altitude, clouds are usually visible below you.
On the eastern side of the island of Molokaʻi lies the Kamakou volcano, leading to a significantly hillier and slightly more vegetated landscape than the western parts of the island.

Kahoʻolawe is a small island that lies just to the southwest of Maui. It only has trekker coverage on small gravel roads and dirt trails, and is characterised by dry, shrubby vegetation, rolling hills, and dark red soil. On the western end of this coverage, several buildings can be seen.

lm.name: Agriculture - Eucalyptus Plantation
lm.note: The north east coast of Hawai'i Island is characterized by planted eucalyptus overlooking the ocean.

lm.name: Car Meta - Stubby Antenna
lm.note: This antenna can be found anywhere, but is most common Hawaii Island, then Kauai, then Oahu.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Gen 2 Hawaii
lm.note: Generation 2 coverage can only be found on the islands of Hawaiʻi, Maui and Oʻahu.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Gen 4 Hawaii
lm.note:
Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the islands of Hawaiʻi, Maui and Oʻahu.

Note by MB: This applies only to Gen 4, not to Smallcam, which can be found everywhere

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Green Blur
lm.note: Within Hawaii, a distinct green blur can only be seen on the island of Oʻahu.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Elevated Railway
lm.note: The only elevated railway in Hawaii is on Oahu island and runs along the HI-99 for the most part, merges into the H-1 interstate and continues to the airport.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - No Tab / Arrow
lm.note: No tab above sign, arrow on the actual sign, unique to Oahu.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - No Tab / No Arrow / Number
lm.note: Basic streetsigns, but with a number below the abbreviation (Rd/St/Pl/...), unique to Kauai.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - No Tab / No Number
lm.note: Basic streetsign, with only the road name, mostly found in Hawaii, rare on Kauai and extremely rare on Oahu and Maui.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - Tab (Empty)
lm.note: Tab above sign, but nothing in it, found in Maui district (which includes Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - Tab / Long Arrow
lm.note: Tab above sign, containing a long arrow, found in Maui district (which includes Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Road Sign - Tab / Short Arrow
lm.note: Tab above sign, containing a short or very short arrow, almost unique to Oahu.

lm.name: Landscape - Central Maui
lm.note: The Island of Maui sits southeast of Molokaʻi. In the centre of the island, you will find somewhat flat grasslands. It has the very recognizable West Maui Mountains to the west, and Haleakala to the east.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Big Island
lm.note:
The coastal areas of the island of Hawai’i are where most of the towns and built-up areas on the island are located. These areas are typically more lush and have more trees and fern plants than the interior.

Note by MB: There is a similar road, the Hana Highway on Maui, which is more narrow and has narrower shoulders than the typical road on Hawai'i.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Lana'i
lm.note: Towards the coasts of the island of Lānaʻi, hills dotted with dry grass and shrubby vegetation are commonly seen. These areas are very rural with few buildings.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Maui
lm.note: Coastal areas of Maui are noticeably lush and green. Banana plants, palm trees, and views of the mountains are all common.

lm.name: Landscape - East Molokai Volcano
lm.note:
Rather flat and wide volcano, making it's shape quite unique.

As the name suggests, it's found in the East of Moloka'i island.

lm.name: Landscape - Flat Forest
lm.note: Rural roads going through forests within a flat landscape are commonly found south of the city of Hilo, on the island of Hawaiʻi.

lm.name: Landscape - Haleakala Foothills
lm.note: The area near Kula is at the foot of Haleakala and often looks over the rest of the island.

lm.name: Landscape - Hana Highway (North)
lm.note:
The Hana Highway runs along the coast of Maui and is narrow and lush in the North.

Note by MB: Note that unlike in the picture, Hana Highway also has center lines on some parts. That creates a possible toss-up with Hawai'i island. However, Hana Highway is more narrow and has very narrow shoulders, unlike most roads on Hawai'i.

lm.name: Landscape - Hana Highway (South)
lm.note:
The Hana Highway runs along the coast of Maui and is narrow. In the south, the landscape is fairly open and you can often see the southern coast, as no trees are in the way.

Note by MB: Note that unlike in the picture, Hana Highway also has center lines on some parts. That creates a possible toss-up with Hawai'i island. However, Hana Highway is more narrow and has very narrow shoulders, unlike most roads on Hawai'i.

lm.name: Landscape - Hawaiian Lattice
lm.note: The infamous 'Hawaiian lattice' can be recognized by the volcanic soil and rocks that are abundant in the region. Volcanic vegetation can also be seen lining the roads. Note that the angle of the roads is a big clue for the area, and that this lattice was built on the slope of Mauna Loa.

lm.name: Landscape - Hilo
lm.note:
Hilo fits nicely into the coastal Hawai'i landscape (lush and somewhat built up). What makes it unique is the grid format of many of its roads. You can also sometimes see Mauna Kea in the west.

Note by MB: Other grids also exist on Hawaii island (notably Hawaiian Lattice, and the area south of Hilo), but they look very different. Each has their own meta describing them.

lm.name: Landscape - Honolulu
lm.note: Honolulu, located on southern Oʻahu, is by far the largest city and urban area in Hawaii. If you are in a dense urban area and can see tall buildings, you will always be in or near Honolulu.

lm.name: Landscape - Houses on Hills
lm.note: In most of Hawaii, houses are built on flat plains. If you see Houses on hillsides, you are most likely around the Ko'olau range in eastern Oahu, often in suburbs of Honolulu.

lm.name: Landscape - Hualalai
lm.note: Hualalaei (a large mountain) rises to the east of Kona.

lm.name: Landscape - Interior Big Island
lm.note:
The Island of Hawai’i (also referred to as The Big Island) is both the largest and farthest southeast island with Street View coverage in the state. The interior areas feature rolling, grassy plains and volcanic rocks. You can typically see one or more of the island’s volcanoes from the road.

What sets apart the mountains on this island is that they are more sloping and gradual than on other islands.

lm.name: Landscape - Kauai
lm.note:
The Island of Kauai is the furthest west island in Hawaii with official Google coverage. This island has deep red soil and has large rugged hills with lush, jungle-like vegetation. This island also has exclusively Generation 3 and Smallcam coverage.

NOTE: Other islands such as Maui and Molokaʻi have similar soil colours, but the hillsides on them will typically have less dense vegetation.

lm.name: Landscape - Kaunakakai
lm.note: The town of Kaunakakai is the largest settlement on the Island of Molokaʻi. It is the only area on the island with an ‘urban’ vibe.

lm.name: Landscape - Lana'i
lm.note: The Island of Lānaʻi is a small, yet distinct island that lies just south of Moloka’i. A volcano is found just east of the centre of the island, adjacent to the town of Lānaʻi. In this area, tall Cook pines are abundant. In addition, some main roads near the centre of the island are lined with younger Cook pines.

lm.name: Landscape - Maui West Coast
lm.note: West Maui can often see Molokai and/or Lanai to the west. The northern part of the west coast has the West Maui Mountains rising to the east.

lm.name: Landscape - Mauna Loa Observatory Road
lm.note:
This road "looks like Mars", and has large volcanic rocks on its sides.

Note by MB: Unlike the road on Red Hill, this road does not have center lines.

lm.name: Landscape - Moloka'i
lm.note:
The Island of Molokaʻi is just southeast of the Island of Oʻahu. This island features deep red soil, dry-looking vegetation, and a prominent volcano on the eastern end of the island. Molokaʻi is also very sparsely populated. This island only has Generation 3 and Smallcam coverage.

Note by MB: In the newest smallcam coverage, the island doesn't look as dry as in Gen 3 (due to different season).

lm.name: Landscape - O'ahu
lm.note: The Island of Oʻahu lies southeast of Kauai. It is known for being home to the Honolulu urban area. It also is home to steep, lush hills, which can be commonly seen from all around the island, especially in Honolulu’s suburbs. Generation 4 coverage is common on Oʻahu.

lm.name: Landscape - Red Hill
lm.note:
The Red Hill can easily be recognised by this unique barren, rocky landscape. Due to the high altitude, clouds are usually visible below you.

Note by MB: In newer smallcam coverage the hill looks not that red, but the coverage is still recognizable. Also, unlike the Mauna Lea observatory road on Hawai'i, this road has yellow center lines.

lm.name: Landscape - Seaview Road
lm.note: The road around and east of Seaview (Hawai'i island) is very distinct, as it combines the volcanic rock landscape with water immediately to the South.

lm.name: Landscape - Volcanic Rock
lm.note: Hawaii island has the only currently active volcano and is the most recently formed island, so lots of volcanic rock is common.

lm.name: Misc - North-West Road Angle
lm.note: A weirdly good meta for the Kona area (western Hawai'i) is roads that are angled SE-NW.

lm.name: Misc - Oahu Area Codes
lm.note:
Signs on Oahu (and sometimes other places) often have a 2-digit number followed by a dash. These correspond to different tax zones.

They are not used in urban Honolulu. They start with 41 at the east coast, and increase counter-clockwise along the coast.
